parts.latex:
A bag contains six balls numbered 1 to 6. One ball is drawn from the bag and replaced back into the bag. A second ball is then drawn from the bag.

Which of the following outcomes is LEAST likely to occur?

solutions.latex:
Drawing with replacement gives $6\times 6 = 36$ equally likely outcomes. Count the outcomes for each option.

Option A: sum of 5.
$$(1,4),\ (2,3),\ (3,2),\ (4,1)$$
This is 4 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{4}{36}$.

Option B: one odd and one even. There are 3 odd and 3 even numbers, and either order is allowed.
$$2\times 3\times 3 = 18 \text{ outcomes}$$
So $P = \dfrac{18}{36}$.

Option C: the same number.
$$(1,1),\ (2,2),\ \dots,\ (6,6)$$
This is 6 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{6}{36}$.

Option D: differ by 2.
$$(1,3),\ (2,4),\ (3,5),\ (4,6)$$
Each can be reversed, giving 8 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{8}{36}$.

The smallest probability is $\dfrac{4}{36}$, so the least likely outcome is the sum of 5.

meta.self_check: Counted outcomes out of 36: A 4, B 18, C 6, D 8; minimum is A, matching the key.

6472.stem: At a local fast food restaurant, the probability, $W$, of the ice cream machine working on any given day is $40\%$. Ronald visits the restaurant on three consecutive days attempting to order an ice cream.

parts.latex: Find the probability that Ronald only successfully orders an ice cream on one out of three visits to the restaurant.

criteria: Finds the probability of the ice cream machine working on all three days, or equivalent merit
Completes the tree diagram, or equivalent merit

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
There are three orders in which the machine works on exactly one day, each with the same probability.
$$\begin{aligned}P(W\text{ on one day only})&=P(W\overline{W}\,\overline{W})+P(\overline{W}W\overline{W})+P(\overline{W}\,\overline{W}W)\\&=3\times 0.4\times 0.6\times 0.6\\&=0.432\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the probability of one of the three possible outcomes, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Chris has eight blue socks and seven white socks in his drawer. He is rushing while getting ready for work and, without looking, randomly selects two socks from the drawer.

What is the probability that Chris chooses two socks that are the same colour?

solutions.latex:
There are $15$ socks in total. The socks are the same colour if both are blue or both are white (without replacement).

$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{same colour})&=P(BB)+P(WW)\\ &=\dfrac{8}{15}\times\dfrac{7}{14}+\dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{6}{14}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{15}+\dfrac{1}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P=\dfrac{7}{15}$$
criteria: Finds the probability of either both blue or both white socks and attempts to find the second probability, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A dish is selected at random. What is the probability that it is a cashew tofu meal?

An Uber driver picks up 2 dishes from the restaurant for delivery

Construct a tree diagram of the possible outcomes and correctly write the probability on each branch.
Show that the probability of the two dishes being the same is $\dfrac{14}{45}$?
The Uber drive picks up 2 dishes from your restaurant for 20 consecutive days. On how many days would the driver expect to have two different dishes?

solutions.latex:
There are 2 cashew tofu dishes out of 10.
$$P(T) = \dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{1}{5}$$

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
The first dish is chosen from 10, the second from the remaining 9.

First dish: $S = \dfrac{5}{10}$, $P = \dfrac{3}{10}$, $T = \dfrac{2}{10}$.

Second dish after S: $\dfrac49, \dfrac39, \dfrac29$.

Second dish after P: $\dfrac59, \dfrac29, \dfrac29$.

Second dish after T: $\dfrac59, \dfrac39, \dfrac19$.

\exfigure{715_q8_s1}
criteria: First-dish branches correct, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: Second dish after P is listed as 5/9, 2/9, 2/9 in the source, which sums to 1 but the P branch should be 5/9, 3/9... check: after P, S = 5/9, P = 2/9, T = 2/9 (sums to 1), consistent.
meta.format_note: Source branch values checked: each set sums to 1.

solutions.latex:
The dishes are the same if both are S, both P or both T.
$$\begin{aligned} P(SS) &= \dfrac{5}{10}\times\dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{20}{90} \\ P(PP) &= \dfrac{3}{10}\times\dfrac{2}{9} = \dfrac{6}{90} \\ P(TT) &= \dfrac{2}{10}\times\dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{2}{90} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same}) &= \dfrac{20}{90}+\dfrac{6}{90}+\dfrac{2}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{28}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{14}{45} \end{aligned}$$

Different dishes is the complement of the same dishes.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different}) &= 1-\dfrac{14}{45} \\ &= \dfrac{31}{45} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Expected frequency} &= \dfrac{31}{45}\times 20 \\ &= 13.7\dot{7} \\ &\approx 14 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Probability of different dishes, or equivalent merit
